entry.title: Building a vLLM-style paged KV cache from scratch

link.title: Building a vLLM-style paged KV cache from scratch

entry.content:
Training a language model and serving one are different problems. Training is one big, regular batch. Serving is a stream of requests that arrive at random times, have different prompt lengths, and stop at different points. vLLM and continuous-batching servers exist because a naive server handles that badly.

I wanted to understand those systems properly, so I rebuilt the main ideas from scratch in tinyinfer. It uses plain PyTorch, runs on a CPU, and serves a 1.6M-parameter GPT I trained myself. The goal was never to beat vLLM. It was to build a small, correct version of each idea and measure what each one actually buys.

Three problems a naive server has

  1. Memory fragmentation. Every request’s KV cache grows by one token per step, and you don’t know its final length. If you reserve the worst case up front (prompt + max_new_tokens), most of that reservation is never used, and it limits how many requests fit at once.
  2. Head-of-line blocking. With static batches, a short request that lands in the same batch as a long one waits for the long one to finish.
  3. Redundant work. Many requests start with the same system prompt, and recomputing its KV cache for every request is wasted compute.

Idea 1: page the KV cache like an operating system

Instead of one contiguous tensor per request, the cache is a shared pool of fixed-size blocks of 16 tokens (vLLM’s default). Each request gets a block table that maps its logical token positions to physical blocks, the same way a page table maps virtual addresses to page frames. Blocks are allocated only when a request actually needs one.

The trick that kept the code simple is flat slot addressing: a token’s location is block_id * block_size + offset. Writing any set of tokens is then a single index_copy_, and reading them is a single index_select. My first version gathered K/V with a Python list comprehension over (block, offset) pairs, and the vectorized gather alone made the per-request loop noticeably faster.

The naive baseline reuses the same classes with block_size = max_seq_len. In other words, contiguous pre-allocation is just paging with one page per sequence, which makes the comparison fair.

On live traffic, the share of reserved KV slots that were never used dropped from 42.8% to 12.0%.

A bug paging surfaced. Cache slots were first reserved once per layer instead of once per token, so with 4 layers the position counter ran 4x too fast. Slots are now reserved once at the model level and shared by every layer. Without the exactness tests (below) I would not have caught it.

Idea 2: decode the whole batch in one forward pass

Continuous batching only pays off if the running requests are actually computed together. decode_batch does one forward pass for all B running requests:

  1. Reserve one slot per request and write the new K/V rows.
  2. Build a padded [B, max_len] grid of each request’s context slots, plus a validity mask.
  3. Gather K/V for the whole grid with one index_select, then run masked attention for the batch.

Every linear layer and MLP then runs as one [B, C] matmul instead of B separate [1, C] calls.

max batch per-request loop (tok/s) batched decode (tok/s) speedup
1 154.0 161.8 1.05x
8 151.9 447.0 2.94x
32 156.9 665.9 4.24x

Compared with the original v1 engine (115.8 tok/s at batch 32), that is about 5.7x.

Idea 3: schedule one step at a time

The continuous scheduler runs a short loop every decode step:

  1. Admit waiting requests while batch slots and KV blocks allow.
  2. Make sure every running request can get a slot for its next token.
  3. Decode the whole batch.
  4. Evict finished requests and free their blocks immediately.

A request that finishes frees its blocks in the same step, and a new request can start in the next step.

The clearest demonstration is one long request (100 tokens) sharing a batch with three short ones (8 tokens):

request naive latency (s) continuous latency (s)
long 0.694 0.689
short ×3 0.694 0.108

Under Poisson traffic at 12 requests/s, the median time to first token went from 0.737 s to 0.019 s. Both engines use the same batched compute, so this difference comes purely from scheduling.

Idea 4: cache shared prefixes by hash

When a block is full, it gets a chained hash: h_i = hash(h_{i-1}, tokens_in_block_i). Because each hash includes the previous one, equal hashes mean an equal entire prefix, not just an equal block.

On admission, the scheduler walks the prompt’s block hashes, adopts every match by reference (ref count + 1), and prefills only the uncached suffix. When the last owner frees a cached block, it isn’t freed immediately. It sits in an LRU list and is reused only when the free list runs out, so caching never takes memory away from live requests.

With a shared 96-token system prompt, the number of prefill tokens computed fell from 6,666 to 618 (−91%), with a 99.7% hit rate.

The honest caveat: throughput didn’t change, and the absolute time-to-first-token gain is small, because prefill on a 1.6M-parameter model is cheap. On a large model with a long system prompt, prefill dominates time to first token, and that is where this saving matters.

Idea 5: admit optimistically, preempt when memory runs out

Reserving the worst case per request is safe but wasteful when requests stop early. The optimistic policy (vLLM’s) admits a request as long as its prompt fits. If a later step needs a block the pool can’t supply, the scheduler preempts the newest running request:

  1. Publish its full blocks to the prefix cache.
  2. Free its memory.
  3. Put it back at the front of the queue.

When it is re-admitted, it re-prefills prompt + generated_so_far, mostly from the cache, and continues exactly where it stopped.

With a tight KV pool, this gave +27% throughput and a running batch 2.1x larger from the same memory, at the cost of 22 preemptions.

Proving that the optimizations change nothing

Every optimization above is only worth having if it is exact. The 26-test suite checks that, under greedy decoding, all of these produce token-for-token the same output as the reference engine:

  • batched decode
  • prefix caching
  • preemption
  • prefix caching together with preemption
  • both admission policies

It also checks that paged prefill and batched decode match the dense model’s logits, and that every block returns to the pool at the end. Writing these tests first made the later refactors much less scary.

What I’d build next

  • Chunked prefill, so a long prompt never stalls the decode batch.
  • A fused paged-attention kernel in Triton, which reads K/V straight from blocks instead of building a padded grid.
  • Speculative decoding, which fits naturally with a batched verifier.
  • A bigger model on a GPU, where every one of these wins grows.

The code, benchmarks and raw results are on GitHub. For background, read the vLLM paper (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023) and the Orca paper (Yu et al., OSDI 2022).
entry.summary: What makes LLM serving fast, rebuilt on a tiny GPT in plain PyTorch, with every optimization measured.

entry.title: Evaluating a signal, not a portfolio: building an alpha tear sheet

link.title: Evaluating a signal, not a portfolio: building an alpha tear sheet

entry.content:
A backtest Sharpe mixes two different things:

  • Signal quality: does the model rank stocks correctly?
  • Portfolio choices: sizing, rebalancing, costs and neutralization.

In my previous post, the same signal swung from a Sharpe of +0.39 to −0.28 purely because of how the portfolio was built. So before building a portfolio, I want to judge the signal on its own. That is the job of an alpha tear sheet.

All numbers below come from my alpha research framework: a pooled LightGBM model on 70 US large caps, tested out-of-sample from January 2018 to July 2026.

1. Information coefficient (IC)

The IC is the Spearman rank correlation, across all stocks on one date, between today’s signal and the forward return that follows. A perfect signal has IC = 1 and noise has IC ≈ 0. In real equity markets, a mean IC of a few hundredths is already considered a useful signal.

Computing it per date and then averaging matters. Pooling every (date, stock) pair would mostly measure market moves, which a neutral book doesn’t trade.

Metric Value
Mean daily rank IC (5-day horizon) 0.0054
Days with positive IC 50.5%
IC t-stat (Newey-West) 0.93

2. Why the t-stat needs Newey-West

With a 5-day forward-return label, the label for Monday and the label for Tuesday share four days of returns. Consecutive daily ICs are therefore autocorrelated. A naive t-stat treats them as independent, which counts the same information several times and overstates significance.

Newey-West (HAC) standard errors correct for this by adding the autocovariances up to a lag. I set the lag to the label horizon. With that correction the t-stat is 0.93, which is not statistically significant on its own. That’s an honest result, and it matches what the overfitting statistics said.

3. IC decay: where does the information live?

Measuring the same signal’s IC against forward returns at several horizons shows how quickly its information fades or builds:

Horizon (days) 1 5 21
Mean IC 0.0023 0.0054 0.0089

The IC rises with horizon. This signal is slow and factor-like, not a short-term reversal effect. That has a direct consequence: trading it daily pays a lot in costs for information that only shows up over weeks. Sure enough, every daily-rebalanced configuration in my grid was the worst.

4. Quantile returns: is it monotone?

Each day, split the stocks into five buckets by signal and record each bucket’s average next-day return. A real signal should look like a staircase, not just one good bucket at one end.

  • Top minus bottom quintile, gross: 8.2% per year
  • Monotonicity (Spearman correlation between bucket rank and bucket return): 0.30

The edge is mostly at the extremes, and the staircase is noisy.

5. Signal autocorrelation: what will turnover cost?

This is the rank correlation between the signal on day t and on day t − 1. It came out at 0.71.

A higher value means a more stable ranking, so you trade less to follow it. At 0.71 the ranking still changes enough day to day that, without smoothing, daily turnover reached about 111%. An exponential moving average of the signal combined with weekly rebalancing brought it down to roughly 20%.

6. Factor attribution

Finally, regress the strategy’s daily returns on known factors, with HAC errors:

  • market
  • momentum
  • short-term reversal

Whatever is left over (the intercept) is the alpha. This regression exposed the hidden market beta of 0.19 in the dollar-neutral book.

7. What the model actually uses

The top features are classic, well-documented anomalies:

  • illiquidity
  • 12-1 momentum
  • beta
  • volatility
  • distance from the 52-week high

That’s reassuring, because the model found known effects rather than noise. It is also humbling, because those effects are weak among mega-caps, and the market already prices them.

Verdict

The signal carries a little real information: positive IC that grows with horizon, a gross quintile spread, and sensible features. It is not enough to survive costs in a 70-stock mega-cap universe once the beta exposure is removed.

The tear sheet lets me say that precisely, instead of “the backtest didn’t work.” Cheaper execution, a broader universe, or slower rebalancing would be the next things to try.

References

  • Grinold & Kahn, Active Portfolio Management: the information coefficient and IC-based evaluation
  • Newey & West (1987): HAC standard errors
entry.summary: IC, Newey-West t-stats, IC decay and quantile spreads, explained one plot at a time.

entry.title: Why my backtest Sharpe was lying

link.title: Why my backtest Sharpe was lying

entry.content:
My first backtest of a cross-sectional ML signal on 70 US large caps showed a net Sharpe of 0.39. That’s not spectacular, but it’s respectable for a market-neutral long/short book on mega-caps. This post explains why that number was wrong and which tools showed it.

The short version:

  • The book had a hidden market beta of 0.19 (t = 7.8).
  • Made truly beta-neutral, the same signal earns a Sharpe of −0.28 after costs.
  • Against the 24 configurations I tried, its Deflated Sharpe Ratio is about 0.
  • 0 of 5 independent out-of-sample paths are profitable.

Everything here comes from my alpha research framework.

The setup

  • Universe: 70 large caps across all 11 GICS sectors, 10 years of daily data.
  • Features: 20 technical features plus 6 classic equity factors (12-1 momentum, distance from the 52-week high, beta, idiosyncratic volatility, Amihud illiquidity, max return). Every feature is ranked across stocks each day.
  • Target: the cross-sectional rank of the 5-day forward return.
  • Model: one pooled LightGBM model across all stocks.
  • Portfolio: long the top quintile, short the bottom quintile, with 7 bps of costs on every trade.

Lie #1: “market-neutral” wasn’t

“Dollar-neutral” means the money on the long side equals the money on the short side. That is not the same as market-neutral. If the longs are high-beta stocks and the shorts are low-beta ones, the book is net long the market even though it is balanced in dollars. Over a bull market, that exposure looks like alpha.

That is exactly what happened. One of the model’s top features was beta_63, so it learned to like high-beta stocks. A regression of daily returns on market, momentum and short-term reversal factors made it obvious:

Same signal, portfolio built as… Net Sharpe Market beta (t) Alpha (t)
Dollar-neutral 0.39 0.19 (7.8) 0.5% (0.19)
Dollar and beta neutral −0.28 0.04 (2.4) −2.9% (−1.10)

The fix is to project the weights so they are orthogonal to both a vector of ones (dollar-neutral) and the vector of betas (beta-neutral). Once that exposure is gone, the edge goes with it.

Lesson: always regress a “neutral” strategy on the market before believing its Sharpe.

Lie #2: one backtest path has no error bar

A walk-forward backtest gives you exactly one equity curve, and one Sharpe ratio with no error bar.

Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV) fixes that:

  1. Split time into 6 groups.
  2. Test on every combination of 2 groups: C(6,2) = 15 splits.
  3. Stitch the splits into 5 complete, independent out-of-sample paths.

Every split is purged of overlapping labels and embargoed, the same as in the walk-forward. The result is a distribution instead of a single number: Sharpe −0.29 ± 0.34, with 0 of 5 paths positive. The loss isn’t caused by one unlucky split.

Lie #3: the best of 24 tries is biased upward

I didn’t run one configuration. I ran a grid of 24:

  • forward-return horizon
  • model
  • portfolio rule
  • quantile cut-off

If you pick the best of 24 and report its Sharpe, you’re reporting the maximum of 24 noisy numbers, which is biased upward even if none of them has any skill.

Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR)

PSR asks: given this track record’s length, skew and fat tails, what’s the probability the true Sharpe is above zero? For the main configuration it was 0.21, so not convincing.

Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR)

DSR raises the bar. It works out the Sharpe you would expect from the luckiest of N strategies with zero skill, using the spread of Sharpes you actually observed, and then asks whether your winner beats that.

With 24 trials, luck alone would be expected to produce a daily Sharpe of about 0.10, roughly 1.6 annualized. The best trial was nowhere near that, so DSR ≈ 0.00.

Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO)

PBO, computed with CSCV over 12,870 splits, asks how often the trial ranked best in-sample ends up in the bottom half out-of-sample. It came out at 0.21, which looks reassuring.

The full picture is more subtle. The trial rankings are stable, mostly because daily rebalancing is always the worst. But the in-sample winner still loses money out-of-sample in 86% of splits. Stable rankings don’t mean profitability.

Before neutralization, the warning signs were already there

Even before I found the beta problem, these tools were sceptical: DSR was 0.02 and PBO was 0.36, while the headline Sharpe looked fine. That gap is the reason to build the tools at all. A single backtest number tells you very little about whether a strategy is real.

Things I’d tell myself before starting

  • Make every leakage control testable. One test feeds the backtester a perfect-foresight signal (it must profit) and a same-day signal (it must not). That proves the P&L uses yesterday’s weights.
  • Record every trial, including the bad ones. You can’t deflate a Sharpe if you’ve forgotten how many things you tried.
  • Costs decide. All 8 daily-rebalanced trials lost heavily at 7 bps, with up to 111% daily turnover. Smoothing the signal and rebalancing weekly cut turnover to about 20% a day, but that still wasn’t enough.
  • Be honest about the limits. The universe has survivorship bias (today’s large caps). The cost model is flat. The 24 trials are correlated, so the deflation is somewhat conservative.

The signal does have a little real information. That is a separate question, which I cover in the next post on the alpha tear sheet.

References

  • Bailey & López de Prado, “The Sharpe Ratio Efficient Frontier” (2012): Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio
  • Bailey & López de Prado, “The Deflated Sharpe Ratio” (2014)
  • Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu, “The Probability of Backtest Overfitting” (2015)
  • López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (2018): purging, embargo, CPCV
entry.summary: A Sharpe of 0.39 that turned out to be hidden market beta, and the statistics I used to catch it, in plain English.

entry.title: When 100% accuracy is a scanner, not a disease: physics features for retinal OCT

link.title: When 100% accuracy is a scanner, not a disease: physics features for retinal OCT

entry.content:
This is the story behind our project course poster at IIT Gandhinagar. I worked with Tejaswini Rathod and Shubhabrata Sarkar, supervised by Prof. Prabhat Munshi.

The course was on non-destructive testing (NDT). The question was whether the physics used to inspect materials can also diagnose retinas, and do it in a way a clinician can read.

The claim we started from

OCT (optical coherence tomography) is the standard retinal scan: a cross-section of the retina built from reflected light. CNNs classify OCT scans very accurately, but they are opaque. They can also learn the scanner’s signature instead of the disease.

A published physics-based engine took a different route:

  • Split each scan into a 15 × 10 grid.
  • In every cell, measure two texture quantities: the KT-1 slope (how texture peaks fade under blur) and the Hurst coefficient (roughness across scales).
  • Classify with a random forest.

It reported 100% healthy-eye triage on the OCTID dataset. Our goal was to test that claim, then build physics features that are explainable and hold up across datasets and scanners.

Step 1: reproduce it, then look at the data

I reproduced the engine from scratch and matched the paper:

  • NORMAL precision and recall: 1.00 / 1.00
  • Overall accuracy: 68.3% (paper: 71%)
  • The same top-15 features (all Hurst), in the same grid rows

Then I looked at the data itself. In OCTID, healthy and diseased scans come from different scanners. Their image sizes don’t even overlap, and every healthy file is a .jpg while every diseased file is a .jpeg. Image size alone separates healthy from diseased with 100% accuracy.

The confound also flows through the physics. The preprocessing upsamples healthy scans by about 1.32× and diseased ones by about 1.0×. Upsampling smooths texture, which raises the Hurst coefficient: the Spearman correlation between upsampling factor and mean H is 0.82.

The strongest test was to shrink the held-out diseased scans to the healthy scans’ width and run the identical pipeline. The trained model then called 63 of 63 of them healthy. The perfect triage was the model recognizing the scanner.

Lesson #1: check acquisition confounds before claiming triage performance.

Step 2: test fairly

I added two more datasets, each from a single scanner:

  • OCTDL (Optovue, 2,064 scans, 7 classes)
  • Kermany (Spectralis, 2,401 scans)

Every split is by patient, so no patient appears in both training and test. The hardest test is cross-scanner: train on Spectralis, test on Optovue.

The evaluation setup:

  • Classifier: logistic regression or LightGBM.
  • Validation: patient-grouped 5-fold CV, repeated 3 times, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.
  • Metric: balanced accuracy, because the classes are imbalanced.

Step 3: physics features at three scales

The new pipeline extracts 171 features in three layers. Every one has a physical meaning.

1. Layer texture (111 features). First trace the inner retinal surface (ILM) and the RPE layer, then flatten the retina so the layers lie horizontal. Next, split it into four anatomical bands: inner retina, outer retina, RPE and choroid. In each band, measure Hurst roughness, KT-1 slope, coherence (how layered the texture is), lacunarity (gappiness) and entropy.

On top of the texture, add direct disease measurements in micrometres:

  • thickness and foveal dip
  • macular hole gap
  • fluid and bright foci
  • RPE elevation

2. Echo physics, the NDT layer (46 features). Each image column is an A-scan, the same as an ultrasonic echo trace in materials testing. From it we compute:

  • Attenuation: the Beer–Lambert slope of light loss with depth
  • Interface contrast: echo strength at the ILM and RPE, an analogue of a reflection coefficient
  • 6 dB half-max sizing: the size of fluid pockets and holes
  • Shadowing: signal loss behind bright reflectors
  • Speckle statistics

We removed the 8 features that turned out to be scanner-dependent.

3. Boundary geometry, the fractal layer (14 features). This treats the ILM and RPE as coastlines.

The retina as a coastline

If z(x) is the height of a boundary at column x, a self-affine curve satisfies

E |z(x + d) − z(x)| ∝ dH  ⇒  D = 2 − H

Here H is the Hurst exponent and D is the fractal dimension: 1 for a straight line, about 1.25 for Britain’s coastline, and 2 for a curve that fills the plane.

Before trusting the estimators, we checked them on shapes with known answers:

  • Sierpiński carpet: measured 1.8928, true value log 8 / log 3 = 1.8928
  • Koch curve: measured 1.267, true value 1.262
  • Boundary Hurst estimator: within ±0.01 on synthetic Brownian profiles

The same checks confirmed the resampling confound: 1.32× upsampling raises the original engine’s H by up to 0.04.

Results

Task Chance Physics features (ours)
OCTID: CSR / DR / MH 0.33 0.868
OCTDL: 7 classes 0.14 0.682
Kermany: CNV / DME / drusen 0.33 0.726
Spectralis → Optovue (cross-scanner) 0.33 0.671 (original engine 0.378)
  • Beats the original engine everywhere: +0.13 to +0.36 balanced accuracy over the original engine on every task.
  • Holds up across scanners: 0.671 balanced accuracy, and 84% of healthy Optovue eyes recognized, after training only on Spectralis.
  • NDT features help a little, and consistently: +0.01 to +0.04, positive in 22 of 24 paired tests.
  • A CNN is still more accurate: a fine-tuned ResNet-18 on the same folds reaches 0.86–0.94.

What the fractal features add (and don’t)

  • Meaningful: epiretinal membrane has the highest ILM fractal dimension (1.16 vs 1.10 healthy). AMD and vascular occlusions roughen the RPE (4–5 vs 2.7 µm per column).
  • Scanner-stable: between healthy eyes on the two scanners, the effect size is |d| ≤ 0.58. The strongest NDT contrasts are about 1.5.
  • Redundant for accuracy: on their own they reach 2–3× chance (0.672 on OCTID, 0.533 across scanners). Added on top of texture and NDT features, they change accuracy by −0.015 to +0.020, which isn’t significant.

They explain; they don’t add accuracy.

Take-aways

  1. Check acquisition confounds first. A perfect score is a reason to look harder at the data.
  2. Physics at three scales gives 0.68–0.87 balanced accuracy, and a clinician can read every feature.
  3. Fractal dimension is a validated, scanner-stable biomarker for ERM and AMD, but redundant for accuracy.
  4. A CNN is more accurate. Physics features fit best as the explanation layer of a hybrid system, not as a replacement.

Limitations:

  • The boundary tracer is simple and jumps at some foveal pits.
  • The lateral pixel spacing is assumed, not read from the scanner.
  • Only a subset of Kermany was used.

📄 Poster (PDF) · 💻 Code on GitHub · 🗂️ Project page

References

  1. Banerjee, Sarkar, Munshi, Multi-Parametric Retinal Diagnostics: A Deterministic Physics-Based Engine for Tomographic Classification.
  2. Athe, Shakya, Munshi, Luke, Mewes, Flow Meas. Instrum. 33, 2013.
  3. Mandelbrot, The Fractal Geometry of Nature, 1982.
  4. Kermany et al., Cell 172(5), 2018.
  5. Kulyabin et al., OCTDL, Sci. Data 11, 2024.
  6. Gholami et al., OCTID, arXiv:1812.07056.
entry.summary: Reproducing a physics-based OCT classifier, finding the confound behind its perfect triage, and building explainable features that hold up across scanners.

entry.title: Teleoperating a robot arm with an ArUco marker and a pinch gesture

link.title: Teleoperating a robot arm with an ArUco marker and a pinch gesture

entry.content:
My first robotics project at IIT Gandhinagar ran from January to April 2025. I worked on it with Afraz, advised by Prof. Harish Palanthandalam-Madapusi, with guidance from our TAs Isharath and Debojit Das.

The goal: make an Addverb Heal arm copy the motion of a marker in your hand, and open or close its gripper when you pinch your fingers. By the end, it could pick up a cube and drop it in a basket under teleoperation.
entry.summary: RealSense + ArUco for position, MediaPipe for the gripper, Mink IK in MuJoCo, and why the real arm jittered when the simulation didn't.
